$comment: England & Wales, Sports Law - the common-law duty of care between sporting co-participants, and its practical high threshold in fast-moving elite competition. Both cases predate BAILII's HTTP 403 block on direct WebFetch this session; the researching agent used a browser-automation tool to load the full BAILII HTML judgment text instead of WebFetch. Neither judgment carries paragraph numbers (both predate neutral-citation-style numbering), so quotes are identified by speaker rather than pinpoint paragraph.
verification_method: Condon v Basi [1985] EWCA Civ 12 and Caldwell v Maguire [2001] EWCA Civ 1054 both fetched live via BAILII (bailii.org) - direct WebFetch returned HTTP 403 so a browser session was used instead to load and read the full HTML transcripts, not a summary.

authorities.name: Condon v Basi
authorities.judge_or_panel: Sir John Donaldson MR, Stephen Brown LJ, Glidewell J
authorities.proposition: Participants in competitive sport owe one another a duty of care, but the standard is objective only within the circumstances of that particular sport - not the standard that would apply to everyday life - so a higher degree of care is required of a First Division footballer than a Fourth Division footballer, and conduct within a sport's accepted risks does not breach the duty. Adopting Kitto J's approach in the Australian case Rootes v Shelton [1968] ALR 33 (not independently verified in this file). On the facts, a reckless and dangerous late tackle that broke the plaintiff's leg did breach the duty - appeal dismissed, defendant liable.
authorities.verification_note: Fetched live via BAILII this session using a browser-automation tool after direct WebFetch returned HTTP 403 - the full HTML transcript was loaded and read, not summarized externally.

authorities.name: Caldwell v Maguire & Anor
authorities.judge_or_panel: Lord Woolf CJ, Judge LJ, Tuckey LJ (giving the first judgment)
authorities.proposition: Applying and sharpening Condon v Basi in the context of elite, fast-moving professional sport: because split-second decisions under competitive stress are an inevitable feature of the sport, the practical threshold for proving a breach of the co-participant duty of care is high - mere errors of judgment, oversights, or momentary lapses of skill do not amount to negligence, even where the sport's own regulator (here, a Jockey Club stewards' inquiry) has separately found the conduct to be a rule breach ('careless riding'). A regulatory finding does not equate to a finding of civil negligence. On the facts, two professional jockeys whose split-second misjudgment of racing distance seriously injured a fellow jockey were not liable - appeal dismissed.
authorities.verification_note: Fetched live via BAILII this session using the same browser-automation route as Condon v Basi - the full HTML transcript was loaded and read, not summarized externally.

edges.verified_via: Caldwell v Maguire [2001] EWCA Civ 1054, per Tuckey LJ, expressly traces its high-threshold test back to Kitto J's circumstances-based standard 'adopted by Sir John Donaldson MR ... in Condon v Basi [1985] 1 WLR 866,' fetched directly via BAILII.

what_this_is_not: Two verified nodes forming a doctrine-and-application pair on participant duty of care. Does not cover spectator/organiser liability, restraint of trade in player contracts, the 'sporting exception' given to governing bodies' internal disciplinary decisions (e.g. Bradley v Jockey Club), or any other Sports Law subject - all remain unbuilt.
